title: Quantum-State Projectors on Grassmannian: Geometry, Holonomy, and Topology
abstract: An isolated group of $k$ bands in an $N$-level quantum system defines a rank-$k$ spectral projector and hence a map into the complex Grassmannian $\mathrm{Gr}(k,N)$. For a smooth gapped Hamiltonian, this projector is globally smooth and periodic even when band topology obstructs a globally smooth periodic, or symmetry-compatible, Bloch frame. We take the globally defined differential $\dd P$ as the central object: it is the tangent field of the Grassmannian map, removes unphysical rotations within the selected subspace, and retains the physical interband transition. The interband block of this tangent data simultaneously determines the quantum metric and Berry curvature; the associated horizontal generator produces finite Grassmannian motion, while wedge products of $\dd P$ enter topological forms. We construct a shortest path between two projectors in the ambient Grassmannian and show that the singular values of its horizontal generator block are the principal angles between the endpoint subspaces. This construction provides a piecewise-geodesic interpretation of discrete geometric phases. In a separate development, we derive a basis-independent expression for the determinant of a multiband Wilson loop from traces of powers of an ordered projector product, without decomposing a degenerate band multiplet into individual bands. Finally, the same tangent-vector calculus organizes Chern characters, chiral winding numbers, and the time-reversal $\mathbb Z_2$ index. The resulting framework unifies local quantum geometry, finite subspace distance, holonomy, and topology while avoiding global gauge fixing.
summary: The paper introduces a rigorous geometric framework using the Grassmannian manifold to describe quantum subspaces defined by spectral projectors. It shows that physical observables like Berry curvature and topological invariants can be derived from the projector's tangent field ($\dd P$) in a way that is inherently gauge-invariant. This unifies local geometry, distance measures, and global topology for gapped electronic systems.
main_problem: To develop a unified, gauge-invariant geometric framework for characterizing quantum subspaces defined by spectral projectors on the Grassmannian manifold.
main_result: The formalism successfully unifies local quantum geometry (metric/curvature), finite subspace distance (geodesics via principal angles), holonomy, and global topology (Chern characters) using only the projector map $P$.
method: The analysis employs differential geometry on the Grassmannian $	ext{Gr}(k, N)$, utilizing the spectral projector $P$ as a map from parameter space ($\mathbf{k}$) to the manifold. Key tools include tangent-vector calculus and Lie algebra decomposition.
model_or_system: The system involves an isolated group of $k$ bands within an $N$-level quantum system, whose band structure is parameterized by momentum $\mathbf{k}$ on a torus (Brillouin zone). The dynamics are governed by a smooth gapped Hamiltonian.
key_observables: Quantum metric tensor, Berry curvature, principal angles between subspaces, Wilson loop determinant, Chern characters, and the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ index.
important_parameters: The number of bands ($k$), total levels ($N$), and the spectral gap ensuring global smoothness of the projector $P$.
main_assumptions: The existence of a spectral gap is crucial to ensure that the spectral projector $P(k)$ remains globally smooth and periodic, circumventing issues related to gauge fixing.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the spectral projector on $	ext{Gr}(k, N)$, deriving the tangent field $\dd P$, establishing that its interband block yields both metric and curvature information. It then applies this to calculate geodesic distances and derives basis-independent formulas for topological invariants like Wilson loops.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful geometric language (Grassmannian geometry) to analyze topological phases in condensed matter systems, directly linking band structure topology to fundamental concepts of differential geometry, which is highly relevant for understanding robust electronic properties.
